summary: Sets out requirements for a service that lets users prove data existed at a given time and has not been changed since, even over very long periods. It also covers verifying signatures after long gaps. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: If you keep an important paper for fifty years, you must be able to prove it was not changed. This lists what a digital archive must do to give that proof.

subtitle: Requirements for digital archive systems that preserve data and prove its integrity for decades or centuries.

tldr.problem: Digital data degrades in many ways over time: storage media wear out, file formats become obsolete, cryptographic algorithms become weak, and digital signatures expire. Users need a way to prove that a document existed unchanged at a specific point in time, even 50 years later.
tldr.mechanism: A long-term archive service accepts data and creates evidence records containing timestamps, cryptographic proofs, and verification data. It periodically refreshes this evidence and migrates data to new storage media, maintaining a chain of evidence that survives cryptographic breakthroughs and format obsolescence.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now prove the authenticity and integrity of important documents like contracts, medical records, and legal filings even after decades have passed and the original signatures and algorithms have become untrustworthy.

facts.label: Primary threat addressed
facts.value: Undetected loss of data integrity over long periods

facts.label: Evidence components
facts.value: Timestamps, hashes, certificates, revocation info, policies

facts.label: Archival period
facts.value: Configurable; examples range from decades to centuries

facts.label: Key principle
facts.value: Non-repudiation of data existence and integrity

today: RFC 4810 is an Informational RFC that defines requirements for long-term digital archive services. It forms the foundation for protocol standards and implementations designed to preserve digital evidence for legal and organizational purposes over extended time periods.

sections.title: The Problem with Digital Permanence
sections.content:
Digital documents face threats that paper does not. Storage media deteriorate, cryptographic algorithms become weak as computing power grows, and file formats stop being supported as software evolves. A contract stored today may become unreadable in 30 years, or if it was digitally signed, the signature may no longer be verifiable because the algorithm is broken or the signing certificate has expired.

A long-term archive service is a specialized service designed to preserve data for decades or centuries. It continuously monitors the strength of the cryptographic protections on stored data and refreshes them before they become weak. It migrates data to new storage media before old media fail. And it maintains a detailed chain of evidence proving that the data has not been altered in its care.
sections.eli5: Paper lasts for centuries, but digital data is fragile. Hard drives fail, formats become obsolete, and the passwords that protect old files might be cracked. An archive service is like a vault that keeps refreshing everything inside to keep it safe forever.

sections.title: What a Long-Term Archive Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC sets out seven major functional requirements. First, the service must allow clients to submit data for preservation, retrieve it later, and delete it if authorized. The service must authenticate requests and confirm that data was received correctly.

Second, the service must operate according to a long-term archive policy that specifies how long data will be kept, what preservation activities will be performed, who can access the data, and what formats are acceptable. Third, the service must allow management of stored data, including specifying the archival period, extending it, and attaching metadata like author, date, and classification.

Fourth, the service must create and maintain evidence records containing timestamps, cryptographic hashes, and verification data that prove the data existed and has not changed. Fifth, it must support encrypted data such that preservation activities apply to the original unencrypted content. Sixth, it must allow transfer of data and evidence between services, so if one archive closes it can hand off to another. Finally, it should support archiving groups of related objects together.
sections.eli5: An archive needs to accept data, store it safely, prove it has not changed, keep encrypted secrets confidential, and be able to move data to another archive if needed.

sections.title: Evidence Records and Non-Repudiation
sections.content:
The core innovation of a long-term archive service is the evidence record. This is a collection of proof documents attached to the archived data. An evidence record includes timestamps from a trusted authority proving when the data entered the archive, cryptographic hashes proving the exact contents, public-key certificates for verifying digital signatures, and information about the policies and procedures that were followed.

The goal is non-repudiation – the ability to prove to a court of law or an arbitrator that the data existed at a specific time and has not been altered since. The evidence record must be structured so that any modification to the archived data or even to the evidence record itself can be detected. Over decades, an evidence record may accumulate multiple timestamps and re-hashing with stronger algorithms, creating a chain of evidence that survives even if the original cryptographic methods become obsolete.
sections.eli5: Evidence records are like a trail of notarized statements saying "this document existed on this date, it looked like this, and nobody has changed it." Over time, you add new statements with stronger proof techniques so that even if old proof methods break, the chain still works.

sections.title: Security Over Decades
sections.content:
A long-term archive must address unique security challenges. If an archive service is compromised, an attacker might alter data silently. To prevent this, evidence records must be tamper-evident and must involve independent third parties like time-stamping authorities.

Cryptographic algorithms have a limited useful lifetime. As computers become faster, algorithms that were secure become breakable. Before this happens, the archive must migrate the evidence to use stronger algorithms. For example, if data was originally protected with SHA-1 hashing, the archive must periodically refresh it with SHA-256 or stronger before SHA-1 becomes completely broken.

Certificate revocation poses another challenge: if a certificate used to sign data is revoked, does that invalidate evidence of the data's existence from before the revocation? A long-term archive must collect revocation information at the time the data was archived to preserve the validity of proofs made at that time.
sections.eli5: Attackers might try to change old data without being noticed. Math tricks for locking down data get weaker over time, so an archive must update to stronger tricks before the old ones break. It must also save proof that nobody revoked important signing keys when the data was new.

sections.title: Operation and Service Continuity
sections.content:
Long-term archive services may be implemented internally within an organization or as external services accessible over the Internet. They may use time-stamping services provided by third parties, or they may provide their own. An archive service must work efficiently even with very large amounts of stored data, minimizing repeated access to archived objects and limiting the number of external dependencies.

For continuity, if an archive service must shut down, it must be able to transfer all archived data and evidence to another archive service without losing the value of the evidence. This requires evidence records to be portable and to remain valid when transferred. Similarly, customers might switch providers before the end of an archival period, and the protocol must support seamless migration.
sections.eli5: Archives can be run by companies or inside organizations. When an archive closes down, all the data and proof must be able to move to a new archive without breaking the chain of evidence. It should be designed to work even with billions of stored files.
